content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces the use of an associative memory of the optimization gradients to enhance the meta learning methods for few-short learning. The proposed method saves updating gradients in a memory and retrieval and uses that to update the subsequent few-shot learning tasks. A controller is learned to query the save gradients.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- It is an interesting idea to save the gradient instead of samples in associative memory.
- The proposed method can be applied with different meta-learning based approaches and improve performances of the other meta learning methods on different datasets. 
- The paper is well written and easy to follow.

Weakness
Although saving gradients sounds an interesting idea, the design of the key-value pair is problematic. During normal optimization, the gradients at each layer are calculated based on the current value and the backpropagation from the loss functions. However, in the proposed method, the gradient values are supposed to be retrieved via only the encoded task representation features. It is doubtful whether the proposed method works as claimed and how the module work. When the network and its parameters are at a status different from the history snapshot, is the model valid to obtain the saved gradients as designed? 
Some analyses or empirical studies should be conducted at least on some toy synthetic optimization tasks to prove the model works as claimed instead of working as a kind of “additive” augmentation on features (in a meta learning framework), similar to other memory augmentation methods for few-shot learning.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The whole paper is written clearly, and the approach should be reproduced. 
The basic motivation for saving the gradient is interesting. But it is doubtful whether the model works as claimed. The design of the key-value pairs is not justified very well.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is doubtful whether the model works as claimed – whether the model is really working as querying the gradients. The design of the key-value pairs does not support it. And additional analyses for proving it are missing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to store past gradients in a key-value storage and use a transformer to aggregate them to combine with the current gradient for weight update in few-shot meta-learning. Results showing that it is able to improve MAML, ANIL and Meta-SGD. However, the difference between using a transformer and simple gradient averaging is not significant.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of the paper is that it presents a novel idea of using a key-value storage to maintain historical gradients and improve inner-loop optimization, and the results suggest that the proposed method can improve the MAML family of methods by a noticeable margin.

The main weakness of the paper is that there is no significant difference between the Transformer variant vs. the Mean variant, especially on MAML, where Mean actually wins 3 out of the 4 (though within the confidence bounds). Sometimes the numbers are not bolded and sometimes they are, but even when they are bolded, the confidence bounds between Mean and Transformer still sometimes overlaps (e.g. Meta SGD Aircraft 35.97 +/- 1.41 vs. 36.26 +/- 1.33), raising a concern of fair presentation of results. Bolding issues aside, I do not see significant differences between Mean and Transformer. The reason why this is an issue is that Mean can be viewed as a form of gradient averaging just like momentum (window averaging vs. exponential moving averaging). So if we continue with this reasoning, the gain we see in Table 1 could be entirely due to a different inner loop optimization algorithm that has a higher momentum for smoother updates. To disentangle the effect of a better inner loop optimization vs. a better meta-learned representation, the authors should also try different optimizers with different number of steps at test time (e.g. solving the inner loop till convergence, with X number of steps etc.). For example, the network may as well be trained using MAML during meta-training, but at test time, solve the optimization problem till convergence since Figure 2 suggests that the optimization isn’t converged. Therefore, the results on Page 7 only suggest that window averaging is a better inner optimizer, but not necessarily better representations. Furthermore, the Momentum or Adam optimizer in Figure 1 does not have access to historical gradients from other episodes or not, raising a concern of fair comparison. The authors seem to suggest that this difference is by-design as “these traditional optimizers cannot exploit past inaccurate gradients for few-shot learning,” but realistically there is nothing that prevents one from using momentum from previous episodes in a momentum-based optimizer. It is true that people often discard momentum when switching episodes, but this one-line change should still be investigated here to explore the real causal factor why EMO is better than momentum. I don’t think proposing a simpler model like keeping inter-episodes momentum would hurt the paper but quite the opposite.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper has several clarity issues, detailed below. Overall I suggest the authors use algorithm boxes to clarify what is exactly done during meta-learning and meta-testing.
 
Notation clarity: Upon first read, it was unclear whether EMO was applied in the inner loop or outer loop. In Equation 2, inner loop updates use $\theta$ and $\theta’$. But in Equation 7, it becomes $\theta_{t+1}$ and $\theta_t$. Also Equation 2 only computes one update, but the line above says it does “a few gradient updates”.

Test-time storage: It also wasn’t clear if the storage was still updated during test-time. It shouldn’t, since otherwise it can see other test images and labels in a particular episode. But I just want to confirm since it wasn’t clear in Section 2.3.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an interesting increment of gradient-based meta-learning. However, the contribution of whether this is a better optimization algorithm or meta-learning / representation learning algorithm is unclear. The difference between using the more advanced Transformer variant vs. simple window averaging is not significant, which makes the paper fall back to an optimizer based on gradient averaging. While a simpler model is not a weakness, the paper should instead advocate a simpler story. Therefore, I think the paper in its current state is below the bar for acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an optimizer for the episodic meta-learning setting suited for memory-optimization approache. The method retains the gradients of past tasks in a memory buffer, and is able to recall the gradients that are better suited for inner-loop optimization on a given task. The performance of the method is showcased on a series of experiments on benchmarks such as Meta-Dataset-BTAF and miniImageNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
--------

- The method could be potentially beneficial for improving common optimization-based approaches.

- The performance of the method in terms of accuracy is convincing, as there is a clear improvement in many conditions.

- The overall idea of exploiting gradients of other tasks is interesting and seems novel to me.


Weaknesses
-----------

1) One of the main issues of this paper is that not much space has been dedicated to provide explanations on why it works. The method may just be doing variance reduction over the gradients, if this is the case then there are more efficient ways (in terms of computational complexity) of doing it (e.g. by data/task augmentations). In other words, we have a good grasp on why optimizers like SGD+Momentum and Adam work, but it is not clear why this method provides its benefits. I would like to see a discussion about this point.

2) It is not clear what are the limits of this method in terms of computational complexity. It would be helpful to add a paragraph that discusses time/space complexity. The method needs to store the gradients of the neural network in memory, this is not going to scale well with large architectures. The use of a transformer as an encoder is also concerning from this point of view. It would be great to see a discussion about this point, with a plot/table that shows how storage (e.g. Gigabytes) and computation-time (e.g. MACs) are affected by different design choices.

3) As a corollary of the previous point, it seems to me that the comparison with other optimizers (e.g. Table 5 in appendix) is somehow unfair because not appropriately contextualized. The performance of EMO is superior to SGD and Adam but this comes at a higher cost in terms of computational complexity. It would be more insightful to compare EMO tho these optimizers also in terms of storage (e.g. Gigabytes) and training cost (e.g. MACs).

4) It is not clear how this method should be framed around recent advances in meta-learning and fine-tuning. A major advantage of meta-learning methods is that they are faster to adapt to a new task. For instance, ProtoNets (Snell et al. 2017) can adapt in a single forward pass, and MAML in a few optimization steps. On the other hand, fine-tuning methods like Big-Tranfer (BiT, Kolesnikov et al. 2020) have very high accuracy but are slow to adapt. The proposed method, seems to slightly boost the performance of meta-learners like MAML but at a high cost in terms of adaptation speed. Therefore, a comparison against methods like BiT seems quite important here. In other words, if EMO is expensive in terms of adaptation speed one could use BiT which is much simpler and easier to train and deploy. I would like to see a discussion about this particular point.

5) How is the encoder trained? I could not find this information in the paper. 

6) Figure 2, inner-loop steps. It is not clear to me why there is a difference between MAML (blue line) and MAML+EMO (orange line) in the zero-steps condition. Shouldn't the accuracy be the same if the model has not been updated at all in the inner loop?

7) The way results are reported in the table is misleading. The authors should highlight with bold font the highest scores within error bars. For instance, in Table 4 ARML+EMO scores 59.99+-1.35 on Aircraft, with ARML and TSA-MAML being within error bars (but not highlighted).

8) Minor corrections. There are some problems with the mathematical notation, e.g. M is used for indicating a meta-learner (Section 2.1) and for the memory (Section 2.2.) which is confusing.

References
-----------

Kolesnikov, A., Beyer, L., Zhai, X., Puigcerver, J., Yung, J., Gelly, S., & Houlsby, N. (2020, August). Big transfer (bit): General visual representation learning. In European conference on computer vision (pp. 491-507). Springer, Cham.

Snell, J., Swersky, K., & Zemel, R. (2017). Prototypical networks for few-shot learning. Advances in neural information processing systems, 30.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Regarding clarity, there are minor issues with the notation and some missing pieces of information (see weaknesses). There could be issues with reproducibility, since the system is quite complex but code is not provided. The work is original and novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the method is interesting and it could be potentially beneficial for improving optimization-based method. The empirical results are convincing. However, the paper fails in explaining the limitations of the proposed approach in terms of computational complexity, which seems to be a major issue. A contextualization with respect to recent fine-tuning methods is also missing.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Few-shot learning is challenging due to the limited number of training samples provided. Optimizing a classifier to do well in such a scenario is difficult because of the lack of information.

This paper proposes using episodic memory optimization (EMO) with existing optimization-based episodic learning algorithms. EMO leverages the gradients of similar tasks observed during meta-training to provide additional information for the task at hand. Doing so nudges the classifier in the right direction.

Empirical results included in this paper showcase the efficacy of EMO. It works well for a variety of learning algorithms and benchmark datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. This paper is well-motivated and aims to optimize a classifier for a few-shot task by providing extra information than is already given with the support samples. It does so effectively via the gradients of similar tasks observed during meta-training.

2. While there are many different components to EMO - the encoder, the memory store/controller, and the gradient ingester (episodic gradient memory stochastic gradient descent) - this paper describes them well and mentions the flexibility in design choices.

3. The experimental results are comprehensive. Firstly, they cover most of the different design choices and find the combination that works well. Secondly, they highlight the advantages (and disadvantages) of using EMO. Adding the distribution shift experiments was useful.

Weaknesses:

1. (CRUCIAL) Benchmarking few-shot learning algorithms requires reporting the performance mean and the standard deviation/confidence interval to measure the statistical significance of the results [1]. This paper does not consider the latter. Taking a look at the statistical significance of the results,
transformers seem to be the best aggregator function.

    1. LRU is ideal for MAML and ANIL, while clock is ideal for Meta-SGD. This result might change when there is a distribution shift.

    2. in Table 4, EMO outperforms SOTA in 2/5 datasets, while matching performance on 2/5 of them.

    3. in Table 9, EMO outperforms SOTA in 3/5 datasets, while matching performance on 2/5 of them.

    4. in Table 10, EMO outperforms SOTA in 3/4 datasets, while matching performance on 1/4 of them.

2. (CRUCIAL) Knowing the computational cost of an algorithm is important for its practical use; however, this paper does not contain a discussion on this topic. What is the computational cost of EMO, both during meta-training and meta-testing?

3. (CRUCIAL) The convergence proof is hard to follow for me. Could the authors add a detailed version? I am not sure about its correctness. For instance, how were Eqs. 11 and 17 derived?

4. The statement "the memory will not be helpful or harmful" in Section 4.2, Analysis of episodic memory, is incorrect. When there is a distribution shift, EMO harms performance.

Clarifications:

1. As far as I can tell, the loss function does not include the memory store keys $K_t$'s. How is the transformer in Eq. 4 trained?

2. How does EMO compare with other algorithms that leverage memory?

3. The k in k-nearest neighbours for the memory store/controller is a design choice. What value does it take? How does it impact performance?

4. The clock controller should be described in more detail. Do the authors have an intuition for why the clock memory controller performs well?

5. When does the attempt to add a key-value pair to the memory store happen?

6. Algorithms like Meta-SGD [2] and ARML [3] are used but not described.

[1]	Dhillon et al., 2019. A Baseline for Few-Shot Image Classification.

[2]	Li et al., 2017. Learning to Optimize.

[3]	Yao et al., 2020. Automated Relational Meta-Learning.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper proposes EMO and explains the method and the design choices well. A few details are missing or overlooked (see "Weaknesses" and "Clarifications" above).

I believe there are mistakes in the theoretical part of this paper (the convergence proof), but I would like the authors to provide more details. The experimental contribution is noticeable. EMO boosts the performance of existing optimization-based episodic learning algorithms on different benchmarks, even though the statistical significance of the results is lower than advertised (see "Weaknesses" above).

Additionally, I believe the proposed algorithm is novel as it adds the benefit of using memory to any optimization-based episodic learning algorithm.

Other minor errors:

1. The number of query samples should be a multiple of $N$ (the ways), not $K$ (the shots).

2. Other ways of meta-learning do not involve episodic learning [1, 2]. So this should be called episodic meta-learning rather than meta-learning.

3. Add subscripts denoting the task for preciseness. When a task $\mathcal{T}_t$ is sampled, its support and query sets are $\mathcal{S}_t$ and $\mathcal{Q}_t$ respectively.

4. In Section 2.1, are the number of meta-training tasks $n$ or $N_\mathcal{T}$?

5. In Eq. 3, the first summation should be over the tasks $\mathcal{T}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{T}_n$.

6. In section 2.2, $\mathcal{M}$ was already used as the meta-learner in Section 2.1.

7. In Section 2.2, the memory capacity is $T$ not $t$.

8. The key for task $t$ is $K_t$ not $k^t$ or $k$.

9. Shouldn't the input to the memory controller be the key and value rather than just the key?

10. Shouldn't LRU be least recently used (from the name)? The text reads "the least used or the most recently used".

11. Use \citep for parenthesis and \citet to refer to as a noun.

12. Why are the low values in Table 5 bolded?

[1] Chen et al., 2018. A Closer Look at Few-Shot Classification.

[2] Dhillon et al., 2019. A Baseline for Few-Shot Image Classification.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes EMO and provides experimental results showcasing its efficacy. A few details are missing or overlooked. I believe there are mistakes in the theoretical part of this paper. As a result, I would recommend a "reject" for this paper in its current version. However, I look forward to the authors' responses.

content.title: EMO: Episodic Memory Optimization for  Few-Shot Meta-Learning
content.TL;DR: We propose an episodic memory optimization for meta-learning, which we call EMO, that retains the gradient history of past experienced tasks in external memory.
content.abstract: For few-shot meta-learning, gradient descent optimization is challenging due to the limited number of training samples per task. Inspired by the human ability to recall past learning experiences from the brain’s memory, we propose an episodic memory optimization for meta-learning, which we call EMO, that retains the gradient history of past experienced tasks in external memory. It enables few-shot learning in a memory-augmented way by leveraging the meta-learning setting and learns to retain and recall the learning process of past training tasks for gradient descent optimization. By doing so, EMO nudges the parameter updates in the right direction, even when the gradients provided by a limited number of examples are uninformative. Additionally, we prove theoretically that our algorithm converges for smooth, strongly convex objectives. EMO is generic, flexible, and model agnostic, making it a simple plug-and-play optimizer seamlessly embedded into existing optimization-based meta-learning approaches. Empirically, EMO scales well with most of the few-shot classification benchmarks, and our experiments show that the optimization-based meta-learning method enjoys accelerated convergence and improved performance with EMO.
